Rethinking Routing Exploration
in Modern Mixture-of-Experts

Bingcong Li1,2    Hao Ma2    Michael Muehlebach3,4    Niao He1    Yi Ma2
Abstract

Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models have become an important approach for scaling model parameters. Modern MoE architectures increasingly combine two design choices: fine-grained expert segmentation and shared experts. The former increases expressiveness by enabling more expert combinations at a fixed activation ratio, and the latter introduces experts that are active for every token. We identify an exploration dilemma between these designs: shared experts can make routing less exploratory by reducing the variability of token representations. This conflicts with the greater need for exploration induced by fine-grained expert segmentation due to the combinatorially enlarged routing space. Consequently, the additional expressiveness offered by fine-grained segmentation may not be fully realized in practice. MirrorMoE is proposed to reconcile this exploration dilemma by shrinking the exploration space through token-adaptive suppression of unnecessary experts. MirrorMoE consistently improves performance across model scales. Code is available here.

1 Introduction

Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models have been instrumental in scaling large language models (LLMs) to trillions of parameters and beyond (Lepikhin et al., 2020; Fedus et al., 2022). MoEs adopt a sparse conditional-computation paradigm, where each token activates only a subset of experts, or subnetworks. During pretraining, recent work has shown that MoEs can outperform their dense counterparts under matched total parameter counts, compute, and data budgets (Li et al., 2026). At inference, sparse activation allows computational cost to grow sublinearly with total parameters. Thanks to these advantages, MoEs have become a core architecture underlying model families such as DeepSeek (Dai et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024), Kimi (Team-Kimi, 2025; Team-Kimi, 2026), and Qwen (Team-Qwen, 2024b; Yang et al., 2025), among many others (Jiang et al., 2024; Abdin et al., 2024).

At the core of MoEs is the MoE layer, which consists of a router and EE experts, each implemented as a feedforward network (FFN). For each input token, the router selects KK experts (K<EK<E) for sparse activation (Lepikhin et al., 2020; Fedus et al., 2022). Building on this basic design, recent MoEs have increasingly adopted two notable architectural advances. The first is fine-grained expert segmentation (Team-Kimi, 2026; Liu et al., 2024). Recent MoEs tend to use larger numbers of both total and activated experts, i.e., larger EE and KK. For example, at the same activation ratio K/EK/E, (E,K)=(64,8)(E,K)=(64,8) is often preferred over (E,K)=(8,1)(E,K)=(8,1). Since there are (EK)\binom{E}{K} expert combinations, the latter yields richer routing space for more expressive token representations (Elango et al., 2026). The second advance is shared experts. Activated for every token, shared experts capture common knowledge that would otherwise be learned redundantly by routed experts. This allows routed ones to devote more capacity to specialization. The combination of the above architectural choices have become standard in modern MoEs (Dai et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024; Team-Qwen, 2024b).

This work reexamines the interaction between these two trends from the angle of routing exploration. The goal of exploration is to search for alternative expert combinations during pretraining to identify (near-)optimal routes for each token. On the one hand, realizing the expressive potential of fine-grained expert segmentation requires exploring a combinatorially larger routing space within each MoE layer. For example, the number of expert subsets increases from 88 when (E,K)=(8,1)(E,K)=(8,1) to (648)≈4.4×109{64\choose 8}\approx 4.4\times 10^{9} with (E,K)=(64,8)(E,K)=(64,8), i.e., several orders of magnitude increase. On the other hand, our analysis reveals an asymmetry during pretraining: shared experts dominate the learned token representations, leaving routed experts with less influence on the layer output. Consequently, even activating different routed experts only leads to limited variation in the learned features, making alternative routes harder to distinguish and thereby undermining the goal of exploration.

This exploration dilemma has tangible consequences for shared-expert MoEs. To see this, we train matched MoE models with and without shared experts at 4 scales, ranging from 100M to 2.4B total parameters. At each scale, we fix the total number of experts EE and vary the number of (total) activated experts KK over {6,8,10}\{6,8,10\}. A larger KK simultaneously increases model expressiveness and demands more strategic exploration due to enlarged routing space. As shown in Fig.1, shared experts no longer provide benefits over their non-shared counterparts as KK increases. More strikingly, the performance of shared-expert MoEs can even degrade as KK increases in Figs.1(b) and 1(d), suggesting that the inefficient exploration hinders realization of the additional expressiveness from larger KK.

MirrorMoE is proposed to reconcile the conflicting architecture designs above. It adaptively suppresses routed experts on a token basis, reducing the exploration space to better match the model’s exploration capability. Technically, MirrorMoE is derived by mirroring the routing logits via sign negation, hence its name. As shown in Fig.1, MirrorMoE improves the performance of shared-expert MoEs and attains expressiveness gains from larger KK. In summary, our contributions are as follows:

  1. ❖

    We identify an exploration dilemma in modern MoEs: the enlarged routing space induced by fine-grained expert segmentation demands greater exploration, while shared experts make routing less explorative. As a result, the benefits of shared experts diminish as the routing space grows.

  2. ❖

    We propose MirrorMoE, which adaptively shrinks the exploration space to reconcile competing demands above. MirrorMoE is conceptually simple, and its adaptivity is theoretically characterized.

  3. ❖

    We demonstrate that MirrorMoE addresses the exploration dilemma across MoEs of different scales. On the 2.4B model, MirrorMoE improves pretraining and downstream performance by 0.67 and 1.64 points, respectively. Moreover, it enables shared-expert MoEs to consistently outperform their non-shared counterparts and restores the performance gains from increasing KK; see Fig.1.

1.1 Related work

MoEs. Modern sparse MoEs originated with the sparsely gated MoE layer of Shazeer et al. (2017) and were extended to large-scale Transformers in e.g., Lepikhin et al. (2020); Fedus et al. (2022). Later work focused on improving scalability, stability, and expert specialization. GLaM (Du et al., 2022) demonstrated that sparse language models could scale beyond one trillion parameters, while ST-MoE (Zoph et al., 2022) improved training stability. MoEs have since become widely adopted. Beyond those mentioned earlier, other representative examples include Gemma4, OLMoE and gpt-oss (Team-Gemma, 2026; Muennighoff et al., 2025; Agarwal et al., 2025). Across this development trajectory, two trends have clearly emerged: fine-grained expert segmentation and shared experts.

Tension between expressiveness and pretraining. A growing line of work shows that a model’s expressive capacity may not be readily realized without carefully designed training procedures (Lion et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026; Jha and Reagen, 2026; Wei et al., 2025a). Within the context of MoEs, related evidence is provided by Jin et al. (2024), which augments learnable experts with fixed zero, copy, and constant experts. Although standard FFN experts can, in principle, learn these operations, explicitly incorporating them still improves empirical performance. The benefit of directly defining these operations, rather than learning them through training, suggests that the available expressiveness may not be fully realized in practice. Our work further shows that the additional expressiveness provided by fine-grained expert segmentation is not naturally attained in shared-expert MoEs.

Additional related work on MoE routing and systems is deferred to App.A due to limited space.

2 The Exploration Dilemma in Shared-Expert MoEs

This section first reviews MoEs and then examines the effect of shared experts on exploration.

2.1 MoE recap

MoEs replace the FFN in each Transformer layer with a collection of FFNs, each referred to as an expert. Among EE experts at layer ll, there are two types: SS shared experts {𝒮ℰl,s}s\{{\cal SE}_{l,s}\}_{s}, activated for every token (Liu et al., 2024), and R:=E−SR\!:=\!E\!-\!S routed experts {ℛℰl,e}e\{{\cal RE}_{l,e}\}_{e}, activated in a token-driven manner. We use KK to denote the total number of activated experts, including the shared ones.

For 𝐡ln∈ℝd\mathbf{h}_{l}^{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, the representation of the nn-th token entering the ll-th MoE layer, the routed experts to be activated are selected by a linear projection 𝐆l∈ℝR×d\mathbf{G}_{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{R\times d}, known as the router. The router produces a probability distribution over the routed experts, and those with the highest probabilities are activated. The activated routed experts are collected in 𝒜l​(𝐡ln){\cal A}_{l}(\mathbf{h}_{l}^{n}):

pl,e(𝐡ln)=exp(𝐆l[e,:]𝐡ln)∑j=1Rexp(𝐆l[j,:]𝐡ln),𝒜l(𝐡ln)=𝖳𝗈𝗉K−S({pl,e(𝐡ln)},e∈[R]).\displaystyle p_{l,e}(\mathbf{h}_{l}^{n})=\frac{\exp(\mathbf{G}_{l}[e,:]\mathbf{h}_{l}^{n})}{\sum_{j=1}^{R}\exp(\mathbf{G}_{l}[j,:]\mathbf{h}_{l}^{n})},~~~{\cal A}_{l}(\mathbf{h}_{l}^{n})=\mathsf{Top}_{K-S}\big(\{p_{l,e}(\mathbf{h}_{l}^{n})\},e\in[R]\big). (1)

Here, 𝖳𝗈𝗉K−S​(⋅)\mathsf{Top}_{K-S}(\cdot) deterministically selects K−SK-S experts with the largest probabilities and [R]:={1,…,R}[R]:=\{1,\ldots,R\} denotes all the routed experts. The learned token representation of this layer combines the outputs of both shared and routed experts, where shared experts capture common features and routed experts learn specialized ones, i.e.,

𝐡l+1n=∑s=1S𝒮ℰl,s​(𝐡ln)+∑e∈𝒜l​(𝐡ln)pl,e​(𝐡ln)Z⁡(𝐡ln)⋅ℛℰl,e​(𝐡ln)\displaystyle\mathbf{h}_{l+1}^{n}=\sum_{s=1}^{S}{\cal SE}_{l,s}(\mathbf{h}_{l}^{n})+\sum_{e\in{\cal A}_{l}(\mathbf{h}_{l}^{n})}\frac{p_{l,e}(\mathbf{h}_{l}^{n})}{Z(\mathbf{h}_{l}^{n})}\cdot{\cal RE}_{l,e}(\mathbf{h}_{l}^{n}) (2)

where Z⁡(𝐡ln)=∑j∈𝒜l​(𝐡ln)pl,j​(𝐡ln)Z(\mathbf{h}_{l}^{n})=\sum_{j\in{\cal A}_{l}(\mathbf{h}_{l}^{n})}p_{l,j}(\mathbf{h}_{l}^{n}) renormalizes the weights of the activated experts, as in (Yang et al., 2025) or Z⁡(𝐡ln)=1Z(\mathbf{h}_{l}^{n})=1 as in DeepSeek-MoE and Qwen1.5-MoE (Dai et al., 2024; Muennighoff et al., 2025; Team-Qwen, 2024a). We follow the latter in this paper. Vanilla MoEs without shared experts are recovered when S=0S=0. For convenience, we omit the dependence of pl,ep_{l,e} and 𝒜l{\cal A}_{l} on 𝐡ln\mathbf{h}_{l}^{n}, as well as the token index nn whenever clear from context.

Beyond shared experts, recent MoEs have also shifted toward fine-grained expert segmentation (Liu et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025; Elango et al., 2026). For the same activation ratio, this trend favors configurations such as R=64,K−S=8R=64,K-S=8 over R=8,K−S=1R=8,K-S=1, enabling a combinatorially richer set of expert compositions and, hence, more expressive token representations. However, realizing such expressiveness through pretraining is far from straightforward, where the challenge also stems from the combinatorial expansion of the routing space. Identifying optimal expert combinations therefore requires more exploration. This motivates us to revisit exploration in MoE training.

2.2 Shared experts weaken routing exploration

This subsection reexamines the roles of shared and routed experts, reveals an asymmetry in their learning dynamics, and shows how shared-expert dominance can hinder exploration.

To isolate the impact of shared experts, we compare MoEs with and without them using matching datasets, tokenizers, and configurations. The models in this subsection have 121M activated and 498M total parameters, with E=66E=66 and K=8K=8. We set S=2S\!=\!2 for shared-expert MoEs, while MoEs without shared experts amount to S=0S\!=\!0. Details are deferred to App.B.1. We select checkpoints at 20%20\%, 50%50\%, and 100%100\% of pretraining to represent the early, middle, and final stages, respectively.

Asymmetric training dynamics in shared-expert MoEs. We first ablate individual experts to assess their importance. Specifically, we zero out each expert’s output and measure the resulting perplexity change, Δ​𝖯𝖯𝖫=𝖯𝖯𝖫after−𝖯𝖯𝖫base\Delta\mathsf{PPL}=\mathsf{PPL}_{\mathrm{after}}-\mathsf{PPL}_{\mathrm{base}}. In Fig.2, the two rightmost columns in the right-hand plots correspond to shared experts. Across all three checkpoints, ablating a shared expert leads to a substantially larger perplexity increase than ablating a routed expert. This shows that shared experts play a disproportionately important role in model performance.

Another means to quantify the asymmetric roles of experts is through the so-termed routing criticality, which replaces the learned router with uniform random routing and measures the resulting performance change. We apply this intervention one layer at a time and report the relative perplexity increase, 𝖯𝖯𝖫after−𝖯𝖯𝖫base𝖯𝖯𝖫base\frac{\mathsf{PPL}_{\mathrm{after}}-\mathsf{PPL}_{\mathrm{base}}}{\mathsf{PPL}_{\mathrm{base}}}. Larger values indicate greater dependence on the learned router. As shown in Fig.3(a), uniform routing in the early and middle layers of the shared-expert MoE leads to a much smaller perplexity increase than in standard MoEs. In other words, shared experts in these layers capture such a large fraction of the learned representation that the layers are robust to random routing.

Next, we examine how this asymmetry in expert roles shapes exploration. Exploration aims to discover alternative routes that produce diverse token representations. We therefore quantify exploration by measuring how much the learned representation changes under different routing decisions. Even before this analysis, the asymmetry between shared and routed experts suggests that exploration may be ineffective: if a highly exploratory routing policy, such as uniform routing, barely changes the output of a shared-expert layer, other routing is also unlikely to produce substantially different representations. We next confirm this intuition using two complementary variance metrics, one induced by experts and the other by routers.

Shared experts suppress expert-induced variance. We first quantify how much an MoE layer’s output can vary when different experts are activated. To this end, we introduce the notion of expert variance. Given an input token 𝐡l\mathbf{h}_{l} and its learned output 𝐡l+1\mathbf{h}_{l+1} in (2), we define the expert variance as

𝖤𝗑𝗉𝖾𝗋𝗍𝖵𝖺𝗋l=1R​∑e=1R‖𝐡~l+1,e−𝐡l+1‖2‖𝐡l+1‖2​where​𝐡~l+1,e=∑s=1S𝒮ℰl,s​(𝐡l)+ℛℰl,e​(𝐡l).\displaystyle\mathsf{ExpertVar}_{l}=\frac{1}{R}\sum_{e=1}^{R}\frac{\|\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{l+1,e}-\mathbf{\mathbf{h}}_{l+1}\|^{2}}{\|\mathbf{h}_{l+1}\|^{2}}~~~\text{where}~~~\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{l+1,e}=\sum_{s=1}^{S}{\cal SE}_{l,s}(\mathbf{h}_{l})+{\cal RE}_{l,e}(\mathbf{h}_{l}).

In other words, 𝐡~l+1,e\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{l+1,e} is the representation obtained if only a single expert ee is activated. A larger 𝖤𝗑𝗉𝖾𝗋𝗍𝖵𝖺𝗋l\mathsf{ExpertVar}_{l} indicates that changing routed experts can produce substantially different representations compared to 𝐡l+1\mathbf{\mathbf{h}}_{l+1}, indicating greater potential for exploration. Moreover, 𝖤𝗑𝗉𝖾𝗋𝗍𝖵𝖺𝗋l\mathsf{ExpertVar}_{l} bounds the relative change induced by any routing policies from above if Z⁡(𝐡l)=∑j∈𝒜l​(𝐡l)pl,j​(𝐡l)Z(\mathbf{h}_{l})=\sum_{j\in{\cal A}_{l}(\mathbf{h}_{l})}p_{l,j}(\mathbf{h}_{l}). Let 𝐡^l+1\hat{\mathbf{h}}_{l+1} denote the representation obtained from any set of activated experts and routing probabilities. As shown in App.C.1, we can prove that max𝐡^l+1⁡‖𝐡^l+1−𝐡l+1‖2/‖𝐡l+1‖2≤R⋅𝖤𝗑𝗉𝖾𝗋𝗍𝖵𝖺𝗋l\max_{\hat{\mathbf{h}}_{l+1}}\|\hat{\mathbf{h}}_{l+1}-\mathbf{h}_{l+1}\|^{2}/\|\mathbf{h}_{l+1}\|^{2}\leq R\cdot\mathsf{ExpertVar}_{l}. We evaluate 𝖤𝗑𝗉𝖾𝗋𝗍𝖵𝖺𝗋l\mathsf{ExpertVar}_{l}, averaged over tokens, for every MoE layer in Fig.3(b). Expert variance is smaller across all layers when shared experts are present. This is because shared experts dominate the output, while routed experts can only make relatively small variations. Consequently, shared-expert MoEs are less explorative even with different activated experts.

Shared experts reduce router-induced variance. Next, we show that when routing decisions are sampled from the router’s learned distribution, shared-expert MoEs also produce less variable output features. To this end, we replace deterministic top-(K−S)(K-S) routing in (1) with stochastic expert selection according to the learned routing probabilities. For each token, we independently sample M=256M=256 expert sets and denote the resulting representation of the mm-th sample by 𝐡^l+1​(m)\hat{\mathbf{h}}_{l+1}(m), where m∈[M]m\in[M]. We then define the router-induced variance as

𝖱𝗈𝗎𝗍𝖾𝗋𝖵𝖺𝗋l=1M​∑m‖𝐡^l+1​(m)−𝐡¯l+1‖2‖𝐡¯l+1‖2​where​𝐡¯l+1=1M​∑m𝐡^l+1​(m).\displaystyle\mathsf{RouterVar}_{l}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m}\frac{\|\hat{\mathbf{h}}_{l+1}(m)-\bar{\mathbf{h}}_{l+1}\|^{2}}{\|\bar{\mathbf{h}}_{l+1}\|^{2}}~~~\text{where}~~~\bar{\mathbf{h}}_{l+1}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m}\hat{\mathbf{h}}_{l+1}(m).

A larger 𝖱𝗈𝗎𝗍𝖾𝗋𝖵𝖺𝗋l\mathsf{RouterVar}_{l} indicates that sampling according to the routing distribution is more likely to produce diverse features, and thus more explorative. Fig.3(c) reports 𝖱𝗈𝗎𝗍𝖾𝗋𝖵𝖺𝗋l\mathsf{RouterVar}_{l} averaged over tokens. Because shared experts dominate the layer output, they reduce 𝖱𝗈𝗎𝗍𝖾𝗋𝖵𝖺𝗋l\mathsf{RouterVar}_{l} by approximately an order of magnitude relative to a standard MoE. The stochastic routing above is equivalent to adding Gumbel noise with β=1\beta=1 to the routing logits (Nie et al., 2021). We further evaluate perturbed routing distributions with β∈{0.5,2}\beta\in\{0.5,2\}. Results in App.B.2 exhibit the same trend as Fig.3(c). Thus, even under routing distributions perturbed from the learned one, shared-expert MoEs are less likely to produce diverse representations.

In summary, our diagnosis suggests that exploration faces inherent limitations in shared-expert MoEs.

2.3 Consequences of the exploration dilemma

The preceding discussions reveals a fundamental exploration dilemma in shared-expert MoEs. On the one hand, the combinatorial growth of the routing space induced by fine-grained expert segmentation demands greater exploration to identify (near-)optimal expert combinations. On the other hand, shared experts reduce feature variation, thereby weakening exploration. This mismatch gives rise to several practical inefficiencies. We reveal them by evaluating models ranging from 100M to 2.4B total parameters. We set R∈{64,128}R\in\{64,128\} and S=2S=2 for shared-expert MoEs, and match the total number of experts for MoEs without shared experts. We vary the number of activated experts as K∈{6,8,10}K\in\{6,8,10\}. In this scenario, increasing KK improves expressiveness but also enlarges the exploration space.

Inefficiency 1. Benefits of shared experts are eroded. The first consequence is that shared-expert MoEs do not consistently improve upon standard MoEs. As shown in Fig.1, when KK is small and hence demanding less exploration, shared-expert MoEs outperform their non-shared counterparts. As KK increases, however, the benefits of shared experts diminish or even disappear.

Inefficiency 2. Shared experts can diminish the expressive benefits of increasing KK. Across the four model scales in Fig.1, increasing KK from 66 to 1010 yields perplexity gains of {2.23,1.32,\{2.23,1.32, 1.08,0.87}1.08,0.87\} for MoEs without shared experts. With shared experts, however, these gains drop to {0.29,−0.03,0.58,−0.03}\{0.29,-0.03,0.58,-0.03\}, i.e., negative at two scales. These negative numbers indicate that additional expressiveness from activating more experts is not fully realized with shared experts.

Inefficiency 3. Shared experts slow routing specialization. As shown in Fig.3(a), replacing the learned router with a uniformly random one leads to a steadily increasing relative perplexity gap across training stages for MoEs without shared experts. This is expected as routing becomes increasingly specialized. In contrast, shared-expert MoEs exhibit little increase in this gap between the 20%20\% and 50%50\% checkpoints, suggesting slower routing specialization.

3 MirrorMoE for Pretraining Shared-Expert MoEs

To reconcile this exploration dilemma and mitigate the inefficiencies discussed earlier, we propose MirrorMoE, a simple yet effective pretraining approach tailored to MoEs with shared experts.

3.1 MirrorMoE shrinks the exploration space

One solution to the exploration dilemma is to encourage exploration. However, this can introduce tradeoffs in MoE training, such as reduced stability and increased optimization variance, as further illustrated in App.B.3. We thus take the opposite approach: shrink the routing space to better match the model’s exploration capability.

An intuitive way to view this is through the number of effective expert combinations, which scales with (RK𝖾𝖿𝖿){R\choose K_{\mathsf{eff}}}. We formally define K𝖾𝖿𝖿K_{\mathsf{eff}} in Sec.3.2; for now, it can be understood as the number of functionally active experts induced by the routing method. The routing space is reduced when K𝖾𝖿𝖿<K−SK_{\mathsf{eff}}<K-S. However, as shown by the ablation in Sec.4.3, naively reducing activated experts is suboptimal. MirrorMoE reduces K𝖾𝖿𝖿K_{\mathsf{eff}} by leveraging experts with low routing probabilities. It selects these low-probability experts in a token-adaptive manner but assigns them negligible aggregation weights. They therefore contribute little to the learned token representation and are functionally suppressed, reducing the number of experts that need to be explored. We detail this approach below.

Mirror routing. Recall that 𝐆l\mathbf{G}_{l} denotes the router weights at the ll-th layer, and consider a token representation 𝐡l∈ℝd\mathbf{h}_{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. Mirror routing activates experts according to a new routing probability

pl,e=(1−ρ)exp(𝐆l[e,:]𝐡l)∑j=1Rexp(𝐆l[j,:]𝐡l)⏟:=ξl,e+ρexp(−𝐆l[e,:]𝐡l)∑j=1Rexp(−𝐆l[j,:]𝐡l)⏟:=ζl,e\displaystyle p_{l,e}=(1-\rho)\underbrace{\frac{\exp(\mathbf{G}_{l}[e,:]\mathbf{h}_{l})}{\sum_{j=1}^{R}\exp(\mathbf{G}_{l}[j,:]\mathbf{h}_{l})}}_{:=\xi_{l,e}}+\rho\underbrace{\frac{\exp(-\mathbf{G}_{l}[e,:]\mathbf{h}_{l})}{\sum_{j=1}^{R}\exp(-\mathbf{G}_{l}[j,:]\mathbf{h}_{l})}}_{:=\zeta_{l,e}} (3)

where any ρ∈[0,1]\rho\in[0,1] yields a valid probability distribution. The first term ξl,e\xi_{l,e} is the standard routing distribution and favors experts with larger logits. The second term ζl,e\zeta_{l,e} is obtained by negating the sign of 𝐆l\mathbf{G}_{l}, and therefore favors experts with smaller logits. This sign reversal motivates the name mirror routing. The convex combination of ξl,e\xi_{l,e} and ζl,e\zeta_{l,e} shifts routing probability towards both ends of the logit range. Experts with larger pl,ep_{l,e} are activated

𝒜l​(𝐡l)=𝖳𝗈𝗉K−S​({pl,e},e∈[R]).\displaystyle{\cal A}_{l}(\mathbf{h}_{l})=\mathsf{Top}_{K-S}\big(\{p_{l,e}\},e\in[R]\big). (4)

Mirror aggregation. This is the central mechanism for shrinking the exploration space, where we aggregate the selected experts using the probabilities ξl,e\xi_{l,e} instead of pl,ep_{l,e}

𝐡l+1=∑s=1S𝒮ℰl,s​(𝐡l)+∑e∈𝒜lξl,eZ⁡(𝐡l)​ℛℰl,e​(𝐡l).\displaystyle\mathbf{h}_{l+1}=\sum_{s=1}^{S}{\cal SE}_{l,s}(\mathbf{h}_{l})+\sum_{e\in{\cal A}_{l}}\frac{\xi_{l,e}}{Z(\mathbf{h}_{l})}{\cal RE}_{l,e}(\mathbf{h}_{l}). (5)

Here, we set Z⁡(𝐡l)=1Z(\mathbf{h}_{l})=1, analogous to (2) and consistent with the convention adopted throughout this work. Alternatively, one may use Z⁡(𝐡l)=∑j∈𝒜lξl,jZ(\mathbf{h}_{l})=\sum_{j\in{\cal A}_{l}}\xi_{l,j} to normalize the routing weights over the activated experts. Consequently, even when low-logit experts are activated, they contribute minimally to the representation 𝐡l+1\mathbf{h}_{l+1} and are therefore functionally suppressed, reducing K𝖾𝖿𝖿K_{\mathsf{eff}}. This reduction is adaptive: it is determined by ξl,e\xi_{l,e} and can vary across tokens and layers, as visualized shortly in Sec.3.2. Viewed jointly, MirrorMoE router 𝐆l\mathbf{G}_{l} serves two complementary roles. As in standard routing, it governs exploitation by selecting experts with large logits. More importantly, it leverages small logits, which standard routing discards, to determine how many experts to suppress.

Lastly, we make two practical modifications to the pretraining procedure to further improve performance. First, because permanently suppressing experts could limit the expressiveness of the final model, we gradually anneal ρ\rho to 00 over the course of training in (3). A cosine schedule is found effective in our experiments; see Sec.4.3. This yields a temporally strategic exploration scheme: the routing space gradually expands only after experts have developed more stable specialization.

Second, a modest additional improvement can be achieved by balancing the probabilities ξl,e​(𝐡ln)\xi_{l,e}(\mathbf{h}_{l}^{n}) rather than the mirror-routing probabilities pl,e​(𝐡ln)p_{l,e}(\mathbf{h}_{l}^{n}). Specifically, modify the load-balancing loss to

ℒbal=R​∑l=1L∑e=1Rfl,e​q¯l,e,with​fl,e=cl,eN⁡(K−S),q¯l,e=1N​∑n=1Nξl,e​(𝐡ln)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{bal}}=R\sum_{l=1}^{L}\sum_{e=1}^{R}f_{l,e}\bar{q}_{l,e},~~~\text{with}~~~f_{l,e}=\frac{c_{l,e}}{N(K-S)},~~\bar{q}_{l,e}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\xi_{l,e}(\mathbf{h}_{l}^{n}) (6)

where NN is the number of tokens and cl,ec_{l,e} is the number of tokens routed to expert ee at llth layer. The intuition is that experts with small ξl,e​(𝐡ln)\xi_{l,e}(\mathbf{h}_{l}^{n}) contribute little to the resulting token representations, even if activated. The load-balancing objective therefore focuses on the experts that are functionally active. As shown in App.B.5, this modification improves performance. The complete MirrorMoE pretraining procedure is summarized in Alg.1.

3.2 Visualization of routing space reduction in MirrorMoE

Next, we empirically show that MirrorMoE shrinks the exploration space early in training and ultimately learns a more confident routing policy, indicating stronger expert specialization. The notion of effective experts is introduced to quantify this.

Definition 3.1 ((Token-wise) effective experts).

For a given token 𝐡ln\mathbf{h}_{l}^{n}, recall the mirror aggregation in (5). The effective experts for this token is defined as

K𝖾𝖿𝖿(𝐡ln)=exp(−∑e∈𝒜l​(𝐡ln)ξ¯l,e(𝐡ln)logξ¯l,e(𝐡ln)),whereξ¯l,e(𝐡ln)=ξl,e​(𝐡ln)∑j∈𝒜l​(𝐡ln)ξl,j​(𝐡ln).\displaystyle K_{\mathsf{eff}}(\mathbf{h}_{l}^{n})=\exp\Big(-\sum_{e\in{\cal A}_{l}(\mathbf{h}_{l}^{n})}\bar{\xi}_{l,e}(\mathbf{h}_{l}^{n})\log\bar{\xi}_{l,e}(\mathbf{h}_{l}^{n})\Big),~~\text{where}~~\bar{\xi}_{l,e}(\mathbf{h}_{l}^{n})=\frac{\xi_{l,e}(\mathbf{h}_{l}^{n})}{\sum_{j\in{\cal A}_{l}(\mathbf{h}_{l}^{n})}\xi_{l,j}(\mathbf{h}_{l}^{n})}.

We omit the dependence on 𝐡ln\mathbf{h}_{l}^{n} for convenience. This definition measures how many of the activated experts contribute substantially to the aggregated representation. In other words, K𝖾𝖿𝖿​(𝐡ln)K_{\mathsf{eff}}(\mathbf{h}_{l}^{n}) is a smooth approximation to the number of functionally active experts, excluding shared ones. If ξ¯l,e=1/(K−S)\bar{\xi}_{l,e}=1/(K-S) for every e∈𝒜le\in{\cal A}_{l}, then K𝖾𝖿𝖿=K−SK_{\mathsf{eff}}=K-S, indicating that all routed experts contribute significantly to the aggregation. Conversely, if ξ¯l,e=1\bar{\xi}_{l,e}=1 for one expert and zero for others, then K𝖾𝖿𝖿=1K_{\mathsf{eff}}=1, indicating that the final token representation is determined by a single expert. Intuitively, if roughly K𝖾𝖿𝖿K_{\mathsf{eff}} experts contribute, the number of expert combinations to explore scales as (RK𝖾𝖿𝖿){R\choose K_{\mathsf{eff}}}, and smaller K𝖾𝖿𝖿K_{\mathsf{eff}} corresponds to fewer “active” experts and a smaller effective exploration space.

We plot K𝖾𝖿𝖿K_{\mathsf{eff}}, averaged over all tokens and layers, against iterations in Fig.4. We train an MoE with 100M parameters and vary K∈{6,8,10}K\in\{6,8,10\}. Alongside K𝖾𝖿𝖿K_{\mathsf{eff}}, we report the minimum normalized aggregation weight among the activated experts, mine∈𝒜l⁡ξ¯l,e\min_{e\in{\cal A}_{l}}\bar{\xi}_{l,e}, also averaged over tokens and layers. It can be seen that MirrorMoE has smaller K𝖾𝖿𝖿K_{\mathsf{eff}} than the baseline during the first half of training. Meanwhile, mine∈𝒜l⁡ξ¯l,e\min_{e\in{\cal A}_{l}}\bar{\xi}_{l,e} approaches 00, showing that some activated experts contribute negligibly to the aggregated representation. Together, these results confirm that MirrorMoE reduces exploration space by functionally suppressing activated experts. We further demonstrate that the adaptivity of the suppression in App.B.4 by plotting the layer-wise version of Fig.4. Lastly, as K𝖾𝖿𝖿K_{\mathsf{eff}} is the exponential entropy of the aggregation probabilities, its smaller value at the end of training in Fig.4 shows that MirrorMoE learns a more concentrated routing policy, consistent with stronger expert specialization.

3.3 Discussions on adaptivity of MirrorMoE

Lastly, we theoretically characterize the adaptivity of MirrorMoE by deriving sufficient conditions for both expert suppression and preservation at mirror routing. We begin with the former. When an expert has a sufficiently small ξl,e\xi_{l,e} and ρ\rho is chosen appropriately, MirrorMoE activates this expert but functionally removes it as negligible aggregation weight is assigned. For convenience, we omit the layer index throughout this subsection.

Proposition 3.2 (Sufficient condition for expert suppression).

For a given token, let {ξe}\{\xi_{e}\} and {pe}\{p_{e}\} be probabilities obtained as (3). Let 𝒜p:=𝒜{\cal A}^{p}:={\cal A}, i.e., (4), denote the set of experts activated by MirrorMoE, and define 𝒜ξ:=𝖳𝗈𝗉K−S​({ξe}e=1R){\cal A}^{\xi}:=\mathsf{Top}_{K-S}(\{\xi_{e}\}_{e=1}^{R}) as the set that would be activated under the standard routing probabilities {ξe}\{\xi_{e}\}. Let emin:=arg⁡mine∈[R]⁡ξee_{\min}:=\arg\min_{e\in[R]}\xi_{e} with ξemin=ϵ\xi_{e_{\min}}=\epsilon, and let j:=arg⁡mine∈𝒜ξ⁡ξej:=\arg\min_{e\in{\cal A}^{\xi}}\xi_{e} with ξj=c/R\xi_{j}=c/R. As ϵ→0\epsilon\to 0, ρ>c/(1+c)\rho>c/(1+c) is sufficient for emin∈𝒜p∖𝒜ξe_{\min}\in{\cal A}^{p}\setminus{\cal A}^{\xi}; that is, MirrorMoE activates this expert while functionally suppressing its contribution during aggregation.

This explains the reduced K𝖾𝖿𝖿K_{\mathsf{eff}} as visualized in Fig.4. Next, we show the token adaptivity of MirrorMoE by identifying a regime in which no expert is suppressed. Specifically, when the router is uncertain about its choices, MirrorMoE behaves similarly to standard routing.

Proposition 3.3 (Sufficient condition for expert preservation).

Let ξmax:=maxe∈[R]⁡ξe\xi_{\max}:=\max_{e\in[R]}\xi_{e}, ξmin:=mine∈[R]⁡ξe\xi_{\min}:=\min_{e\in[R]}\xi_{e}, and κ:=(1−ρ)/ρ\kappa\!:=\!\sqrt{(1-\rho)/\rho}. If ξmax/ξmin≤κ\xi_{\max}/\xi_{\min}\leq\kappa, 𝒜p=𝒜ξ{\cal A}^{p}\!=\!{\cal A}^{\xi}. Moreover, with ξ¯e\bar{\xi}_{e} defined in Def.3.1, it satisfies ξ¯e≥1/((K−S)​κ),∀e∈𝒜p\bar{\xi}_{e}\geq 1/((K\!-\!S)\kappa),\forall e\in{\cal A}^{p}, i.e., no selected expert is functionally suppressed.

Another interpretation for MirrorMoE. The above discussions provide an alternative interpretation of MirrorMoE beyond exploration. In MoEs with large EE and KK, not every token may require the full expressiveness from all activated experts. If a token can be learned well using fewer experts, the capacity of remaining experts can be devoted to other tokens. MirrorMoE can therefore be viewed as an approach for tokens to adaptively determine their number of activated experts, where this adaptivity arises from the expert suppression and preservation shown in Props. 3.2 and 3.3, respectively.

4 Numerical Results

This section evaluates the performance of MirrorMoE. Our implementation builds on (Kang et al., 2025) and uses the Megatron-LM framework (Shoeybi et al., 2019) with the DCLM dataset (Li et al., 2024). All experiments are conducted on NVIDIA H100 GPUs. Code is available at https://github.com/BingcongLi/MirrorMoE/tree/main.

4.1 Pretraining performance of MirrorMoE

We evaluate four shared-expert MoEs ranging from 100M to 2.4B total parameters, with R∈{64,128}R\in\{64,128\} experts. For each token, 66 routed experts and S=2S=2 shared experts are activated, yielding K=8K=8. Activated parameters account for 16%16\% to 38%38\% of the total parameters across models. The model configurations are summarized in Tab.1 and detailed in App.B.1.

Perplexity. We first compare the test perplexity of pretrained MoE models in Tab.1. MirrorMoE consistently achieves lower perplexity across all model scales. Notably, MoE-498M-A121M and MoE-625M-A100M use the same hidden dimensions and differ primarily in numbers of layers and experts. Since the number of end-to-end routing paths scales as (E−SK−S)L{E-S\choose K-S}^{L}, where LL denotes the number of sparse layers, MoE-498M-A121M has a larger routing space under our configurations. MirrorMoE also yields a larger performance gain on this model, suggesting that shrinking the routing space is particularly beneficial when the exploration dilemma is more pronounced.

Runtime. MirrorMoE slightly reduces the per-iteration training time despite introducing an additional softmax operation in (3) at each layer. It suggests improved load balance. Note that MoE-100M-A38M is trained on two GPUs, whereas all other models are trained on four.

Downstream tasks. We further demonstrate that the gains of MirrorMoE translate into improved downstream performance on six commonsense reasoning tasks in Tab.2. For the 2.4B model, MirrorMoE improves the average performance by 1.64.

4.2 Comparison under enlarged routing space

Building on the same model configuration, we vary the number of activated experts as K∈{6,8,10}K\in\{6,8,10\}. Increasing KK enables richer expert combinations, thereby enlarging both the exploration space and model expressiveness. As shown in Fig.1, the standard shared-expert MoE is outperformed by its non-shared counterpart at large KK. In contrast, MirrorMoE mitigates the exploration dilemma, enabling the shared-expert model to consistently outperform the non-shared MoE across all tested cases. More importantly, the perplexity of MirrorMoE consistently decreases as KK increases, suggesting that the additional expressiveness enabled by larger KK is realized.

4.3 Additional experiments

We use a MoE-100M-A38M with K=8K=8 (2 shared and 6 routed experts) for ablation study.

Hyperparameters. Fig.5 compares constant, linear, and cosine schedules for ρt\rho_{t} in (3), together with initial values ρ0∈{0.1,0.2,0.4}\rho_{0}\in\{0.1,0.2,0.4\}. A cosine schedule with ρ0=0.4\rho_{0}=0.4 achieves the best performance and is therefore used in all preceding experiments.

Benefit of adaptivity. We demonstrate the importance of token/layer adaptivity in MirrorMoE by comparing it with two simple approaches that also have smaller exploration space. Both begin with fewer activated experts and progressively increase their number. Specifically, we set K=𝗋𝗈𝗎𝗇𝖽⁡(K~t)K=\mathsf{round}(\widetilde{K}_{t}), where K~t\widetilde{K}_{t} increases from 44 to 88 following either a linear or cosine schedule. Here, K~t\widetilde{K}_{t} includes two shared experts, and the initial value K~0=4\widetilde{K}_{0}=4 is informed by the number of effective experts in Fig.4. These baselines use the same KK for all tokens and layers and therefore lack adaptivity compared to MirrorMoE. As shown in Tab.4.1, neither matches the performance of MirrorMoE.

MirrorMoE is tailored to shared-expert MoEs. We additionally apply MirrorMoE to MoEs without shared experts to further validate our motivation based on the exploration dilemma induced by shared experts. As shown in Tab.7 in App.B.6, MirrorMoE performs comparably to vanilla training. This is consistent with our analysis: without shared experts, the exploration dilemma is less pronounced, leaving less need to shrink the exploration space.

5 Conclusion

This work identifies an exploration dilemma in MoEs that combine fine-grained expert segmentation with shared experts. This tension can prevent the additional expressiveness enabled by fine-grained segmentation from being fully realized while also diminishing the benefits of shared experts. To address this, we propose MirrorMoE, which adaptively shrinks the exploration space to better match the model’s exploration capability. MirrorMoE consistently improves performance across scales.

Future direction. Our current approach addresses the exploration dilemma by shrinking the exploration space. A promising future direction is to improve the routing strategy itself for more efficient exploration.

Appendix

Appendix A Additional related work

Expressiveness does not necessarily translate directly into performance. Beyond those we have discussed earlier in Sec.1.1, additional works similarly suggest that the expressive capacity of neural networks may not be fully utilized in practice. For example, [Csordás et al., 2025] shows that many deeper layers in Llama 3.1 70B behave close to identity mappings. Since identity mappings are available “for free”, this motivates redesign of residual connections for scaling deeper [Zhang et al., 2026].

MoE systems. A complementary line of work focuses on efficient MoE systems, including faster and more principled expert parallelism, fine-grained all-to-all communication, and topology-aware communication strategies; see e.g., [Hwang et al., 2023, Liu et al., 2025, Zhang et al., 2025]. These methods aim to improve hardware utilization, communication efficiency, and end-to-end throughput. MirrorMoE is largely orthogonal to these system-level optimizations and can be integrated with them.

Routing in MoEs. A broad line of work studies alternative routing mechanisms for MoEs. Hash Layers [Roller et al., 2021] use hash-based assignments, while BASE Layers [Lewis et al., 2021] and expert-choice routing [Zhou et al., 2022] promote balanced expert utilization through carefully designed token assignments, at the cost of not being strictly autoregressive. Clark et al. [2022] study scaling laws for routed models. Other approaches replace hard top-KK selection with differentiable routing mechanisms [Muqeeth et al., 2023, Wang et al., 2025, Vahidi et al., 2026]. Several works post-train or fine-tune routers to enable token-adaptive computation [Yue et al., 2024, Zeng et al., 2024], while Kang [2025] uses reinforcement learning to improve routing decisions. During pretraining, noisy routing has also been explored to encourage broader expert exploration: Shazeer et al. [2017] introduce Gaussian noise, whereas Nie et al. [2021] use Gumbel noise. Routing has also been explicitly studied for multimodal models [Wei et al., 2025b]. In contrast to approaches that encourage broader exploration, MirrorMoE adaptively suppresses experts to shrink the exploration space. The work of Liang et al. [2026] studies shared experts from an inference perspective, showing that they can hinder expert offloading, partly because shared experts reduce the importance of routed experts. However, their focus is on routing behavior at inference time, whereas we study how shared experts affect routing throughout pretraining.

Appendix B Experimental details

B.1 Training details

The model configurations for the shared-expert MoE baseline and MirrorMoE are summarized in Tab.4. Following Kang et al. [2025], we adopt a Llama-style MoE architecture. We also follow DeepSeekMoE [Dai et al., 2024, Liu et al., 2024] by using a dense FFN in the first Transformer layer, so that the first sparse layer receives sufficiently developed token representations for routing. MoE-100M-A38M is trained on two H100 GPUs, while all other models are trained on four. DCLM dataset [Li et al., 2024] is adopted. We use AdamW for optimization. The learning rate is selected from {1,3,5}×10−4\{1,3,5\}\times 10^{-4} based on performance after 500 training steps on a held-out validation set. We adopt a warmup-stable-decay (WSD) learning-rate schedule. The global batch size is 10241024, with gradient accumulation used to reduce memory consumption.

The model analyzed in Sec.2.2 is MoE-498M-A121M.

For MoEs without shared experts, we convert the shared experts into routed experts to preserve the same total parameter count. Due to implementation constraints in Megatron-LM, this requires a different expert layout across GPUs, i.e., a different expert-parallelism configuration, and consequently a different number of GPUs. Specifically, Megatron-LM requires the number of routed experts to be divisible by the expert-parallelism size. Therefore, configurations with 66 or 130 routed experts use three or five GPUs, respectively. The global batch size consequently differs across configurations, while the total number of training tokens is kept approximately the same to ensure a fair comparison.

B.2 Router Variance under Different Levels of Gumbel Noise

When evaluating 𝖱𝗈𝗎𝗍𝖾𝗋𝖵𝖺𝗋l\mathsf{RouterVar}_{l}, we replace deterministic top-KK (for non-shared MoEs) or top-(K−S)(K-S) (for shared-expert MoEs) routing with stochastic sampling from the learned routing distribution. Such sampling is equivalent to perturbing the routing logits with unit-scale Gumbel noise (β=1\beta=1) and then applying top-KK selection [Kool et al., 2019, Nie et al., 2021]. We further extend this evaluation by defining 𝖱𝗈𝗎𝗍𝖾𝗋𝖵𝖺𝗋lβ\mathsf{RouterVar}_{l}^{\beta}, where the routing logits are perturbed by Gumbel noise parameterized by other β\betas. We consider β∈{0.5,2}\beta\in\{0.5,2\} and report the resulting 𝖱𝗈𝗎𝗍𝖾𝗋𝖵𝖺𝗋lβ\mathsf{RouterVar}_{l}^{\beta} for MoE-498M-A121M model in Fig.6. The same trend persists across these perturbation levels, further showing that shared experts consistently reduce routing-induced variance.

B.3 Increasing Exploration during Pretraining Can Be Tricky

An alternative way to address the exploration dilemma is to encourage greater exploration during pretraining. However, this can be challenging for MoEs because stochastic routing may introduce unstable router dynamics and increased training variance. To examine this tradeoff, we consider two alternative routing strategies under K=8K=8. First, we replace deterministic top-(K−S)(K-S) routing with stochastic sampling of K−SK-S experts, denoted as Sto-(K−S)(K-S) in Tab.5. Second, we deterministically select the top-22 experts and stochastically sample the remaining K−S−2K-S-2 experts, denoted as Top-22 + Sto-(K−S−2)(K-S-2).

As shown in Tab.5, on a MoE-100M-A38M model, deterministic top-(K−S)(K-S) routing performs best, followed by Top-22+Sto-(K−S−2)(K-S-2), while fully stochastic routing performs worst. These results suggest that the additional instability introduced by exploration can outweigh its potential benefits during pretraining. For this reason, MirrorMoE takes the opposite approach by shrinking the exploration space.

B.4 Layer-wise effective experts

Extending Fig.4, Fig.7 reports the layer-wise number of effective experts, averaged over tokens when training an MoE-100M-A38M model. For example, when K=8K=8 in Fig.7(b), Layers 1 and 2 maintain roughly three effective experts during the first half of training, whereas Layer 3 suppresses more aggressively and approaches a single effective expert. In contrast, Layers 7 and 8 are more conservative, retaining around four effective experts. This confirms that MirrorMoE shrinks the exploration space in a layer-adaptive manner.

B.5 On the Load-Balancing Loss

We use an MoE-100M-A38M to compare the standard load-balancing loss with our modified loss in (6). The two objectives differ in whether they balance the mirror routing probabilities {pl,e}e\{p_{l,e}\}_{e} or the original routing probabilities {ξl,e}e\{\xi_{l,e}\}_{e}. As shown in Tab.6, balancing {ξl,e}e\{\xi_{l,e}\}_{e} reduces perplexity, at the cost of a slight increase in per-iteration training time. Since our primary objective is model performance, we adopt the modified load-balancing loss throughout our experiments.

B.6 MirrorMoE performance degrades for MoEs without shared experts

We further evaluate MirrorMoE on MoEs without shared experts. For ease of parallelization, we use E∈{64,128}E\in\{64,128\} and K=8K=8, with slightly adjusted model depths. These results are therefore not directly comparable to those in Tab.1. As shown in Tab.7, without shared experts, MirrorMoE with ρ0=0.4\rho_{0}=0.4 and a cosine schedule performs comparably to standard training, with no significant improvement. This result is consistent with our motivation: when shared experts are absent, the exploration dilemma is less pronounced, leaving less need to shrink the exploration space.

B.7 Comparison with top-pp routing

We additionally compare MirrorMoE with another adaptive routing approach, namely top-pp routing [Huang et al., 2024]. Top-pp routing activates the smallest set of experts whose cumulative probability exceeds pp, where p∈(0,1)p\in(0,1) is a threshold parameter. Intuitively, it also adapts the number of activated experts over training. Early in training, when routing probabilities are relatively uniform, more experts are required to exceed the threshold pp. As routing becomes more concentrated, fewer experts are sufficient.

However, this adaptivity makes a fair comparison challenging. In our experiments, we observe that the average number of activated experts per token decreases over the course of training. As a result, top-pp routing uses different amounts of activated computation at different training stages, making direct comparison with MirrorMoE and the baseline difficult, as both use a fixed number of activated experts. Tab.8 reports the number of activated experts (including shared ones) averaged over layers and tokens for MoE-100M-A38M with K=8K=8 and S=2S=2.

In terms of training performance, we use entropy regularization with a coefficient of 10−410^{-4} for top-pp routing. As shown in Tab.8, even with p=0.6p=0.6, which activates more experts on average, top-pp routing still underperforms MirrorMoE.
